name: Bioconservatism
summary: Bioconservatism urges caution and restraint toward biotechnologies, especially human genetic modification, enhancement and radical life extension. Its adherents hold that human nature, with its limits, vulnerability and mortality, grounds human dignity and flourishing, and that democratic institutions should steer technology rather than let markets or science set the ends.
scope: The profile represents the bioethical current around Leon Kass and the US President's Council on Bioethics, Francis Fukuyama (Our Posthuman Future), Michael Sandel and Jurgen Habermas, as summarised in the Wikipedia article and the SEP entry on enhancement. Because these thinkers range from conservative to social-democratic, positions on general economic, social and foreign-policy questions are mostly left neutral and low confidence; only biotechnology, human nature, dignity and democratic control are stated positions.

keyFigures.name: Leon Kass
keyFigures.role: Bioethicist and chair of the US President's Council on Bioethics, author of Beyond Therapy.

keyFigures.name: Francis Fukuyama
keyFigures.role: Political theorist who argued in Our Posthuman Future that biotechnology threatens human nature and needs democratic regulation.

keyFigures.name: Michael Sandel
keyFigures.role: Philosopher who argues that enhancement erodes humility and the giftedness of life.

sources.usedFor: Scholarly summary of Kass, Sandel, Fukuyama, Habermas and Annas on enhancement and equality.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Bioconservative writers focus on enhancement, not health financing; Habermas and Sandel lean toward public provision while Kass and Fukuyama are mixed, so no common line is documented.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Wage policy is outside the bioconservative literature, and its leading figures span centre-left to neoconservative, so adherents are split.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Kass worries that market demand and consumer desire will drive enhancement technologies unchecked, so adherents resist treating the market as the best allocator in this field; elsewhere it is not addressed.

public-ownership.rationale: Nothing in the bioconservative sources concerns ownership of utilities; the camp is divided between social democrats and conservatives on this.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Not addressed; though adherents do worry about enhancement widening inequality, they take no shared position on tax rates.

unions-good.rationale: Labor organisation is not a bioconservative topic and the figures disagree politically, so no position can be inferred.

property-fundamental.rationale: The literature is silent on property rights; Fukuyama and Kass lean conservative but Habermas and Sandel do not.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Fukuyama argues science and commerce cannot set their own ends and that biotech firms must be bound by democratic regulation, so tighter regulation of biotech corporations is implied, though the statement is general.

cut-welfare.rationale: Welfare policy is not discussed by bioconservatives and its leading voices are split across the spectrum.

worker-ownership.rationale: Not addressed in the bioconservative sources; no shared position among adherents.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Not a bioconservative topic; the camp mixes civil-libertarian and security-minded thinkers.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Kass objects to shortcuts to happiness and mood-altering drugs that bypass effort, so adherents lean against recreational drug use, though legal policy is not set out.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Speech regulation falls outside the bioconservative literature and adherents are split.

strong-leader.rationale: Fukuyama stresses democratic deliberation through elected, informed representatives to govern biotech, which sits poorly with bypassing gridlock; inferred only.

state-harmful.rationale: Bioconservatism relies on the state and democratic institutions to regulate biotechnology, so the claim that the state is unnecessary and harmful is rejected.

limit-guns.rationale: Gun policy is unrelated to the bioconservative literature; adherents differ.

empower-police-military.rationale: Not addressed; no shared position in the sources.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Kass's emphasis on dignity and on human relationships not being treated as instruments suggests adherents lean against commercial sex, but this is inferred.

decide-locally.rationale: Fukuyama calls for national and international rules on biotech, which cuts against purely local decision, but the general question of decentralisation is not addressed.

rehabilitation.rationale: Penal policy is not covered by the sources and adherents are split.

traditional-family.rationale: Kass defends natural procreation and the generational family against technological reproduction, which supports the family's central role, but he and others do not endorse a single family model.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Kass leans conservative while Habermas and Sandel are liberal, so adherents are genuinely split and the sources do not address it.

abortion-legal.rationale: Fukuyama gives embryos higher moral status than ordinary cells yet is not an absolutist, and Habermas and Sandel differ; adherents are split.

more-religion-public.rationale: Bioconservatism draws on both religious and secular arguments for dignity; Habermas and Fukuyama argue on secular grounds, so no shared position.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Not a bioconservative concern; the camp spans left and right.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Fukuyama defends species-typical human nature as rooted in biology and rejects pure social construction, so adherents lean to disagree, though the topic is not central.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Not addressed; the camp's liberal and conservative members differ.

gradual-change.rationale: Kass and Fukuyama counsel caution toward rapid technological change and respect for inherited human limits, which supports gradualism on the matters they discuss.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Immigration is unrelated to the bioconservative sources; no shared position.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Fukuyama and Annas want international regulation of biotech, but wider empowerment of the UN is not a bioconservative claim, so adherents split.

free-trade.rationale: Not addressed by the sources; no common line.

nation-first.rationale: Bioconservatives want biotech rules harmonised internationally and treaties such as Annas's species-protection proposal, which leans against a pure nation-first stance; inferred.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Foreign policy is outside the literature and adherents differ.

limit-growth.rationale: Not addressed; some adherents share ecological sensibilities about nature and limits but no explicit claim exists.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; no shared position.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Bioconservatism is defined by caution toward technologies that can compromise human dignity, chiefly biotechnology and enhancement; it is not opposed to technology in general.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Energy policy is not part of the literature.

revolution-justified.rationale: Bioconservatives defend democratic, institutionalised control of change, so revolutionary politics sits poorly with them, but it is not discussed.

experts-over-public.rationale: Fukuyama insists that science cannot set its own ends and that biotech should be decided by the democratic community, not scientists alone; inferred for expertise generally.

central-planning.rationale: Fukuyama accepts regulation but worries about overregulation stifling innovation; full central planning is not a bioconservative position and is inferred disagreement.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Not addressed by the sources; adherents are split.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Fukuyama favours state institutions sorting beneficial from harmful biotech, but directing investment generally is not a bioconservative claim.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Not addressed; bioconservatives are not radical economic revolutionaries and would not seek to abolish money, an inference from their institutional caution.

one-party-rule.rationale: Fukuyama and Habermas ground biotech governance in democratic deliberation, so rule by a single party is rejected; the point is inferred rather than stated.

democracy-best.rationale: Fukuyama says legitimate uses of science should be decided democratically by elected, informed representatives and Habermas ties his case to democratic moral equality; the 'even when voters choose badly' clause tempers this.

direct-votes.rationale: Fukuyama favours decisions through elected, scientifically informed representatives rather than direct votes, so adherents lean to disagree.

workers-councils.rationale: Bioconservatives work within democratic representative institutions; workers' councils are not part of their case and are inferred as unwelcome.

natural-rulers.rationale: Habermas and Sandel stress moral equality and Kass rejects engineered hierarchies, so a doctrine of natural rulers is unwelcome; inferred.

war-builds-character.rationale: The sources do not discuss war, but their stress on dignity and caution makes glorifying war unlikely; inferred.

separate-church-state.rationale: Adherents are split between religious and secular grounds and the sources do not address it.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Fukuyama and Habermas deliberately argue on secular grounds for regulation, and Kass uses humanistic reasoning, so scripture-based law is not the norm; inferred.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Bioconservatism relies on state and international institutions as guardians, so privatised courts and defence run against it; inferred.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Fukuyama grounds dignity in the shared human endowment (Factor X), universalist rather than ethnic; inferred.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Not addressed; adherents range from Marxist-influenced to conservative.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Not addressed directly; equality worries about enhancement exist but not about outcomes generally.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Kass criticises the pursuit of individual desire through technology and emphasises limits, gratitude and obligation to the young, so adherents lean against self-interest as a moral good; inferred.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Kass and Sandel stress obligation, gratitude and community while Habermas stresses rights, so adherents are split.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Bioconservatives defend the natural as a moral category, including human nature shaped by evolution, which supports valuing nature in itself, although they speak mostly of human nature. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Adherents warn against technological trends but do not call industrial civilisation a disaster; they accept medicine and therapy, so mild disagreement is inferred.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Bioconservatism urges caution and restraint toward biotechnologies and opposes transhumanism and the singularity, so speeding technological change despite disruption is rejected.

human-enhancement.rationale: Kass argues that enhancement bypasses effort, erodes human nature and makes achievements not fully our own, and bioconservatives broadly oppose it beyond therapy.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Fukuyama wants human, democratic control of technology and Bostrom lists strong AI among things bioconservatives oppose, so handing government to algorithms is rejected; inferred.

restore-past-order.rationale: Kass is conservative about human nature but does not call for restoring a lost social order; the camp is mixed.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Not addressed; adherents hold principled commitments on dignity that a pure results test would not capture, but no explicit stance.

direct-action.rationale: Bioconservatives expect change through democratic law and institutions, which makes direct action an unlikely preference; inferred.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Bioconservatives accept medicine and technology used for healing and defend civilisation's human goods, so abandoning it for foraging is not part of their view.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Not addressed; inferred disagreement from their non-radical orientation.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Not addressed; the camp contains Habermas but also Fukuyama, who reject neither profit nor Marxism uniformly.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Bioconservative governance rests on democratic deliberation and rights; class dictatorship is foreign to it (inferred).

collective-farming.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from non-radical stance.

taxation-theft.rationale: Bioconservatives expect the state to fund and run regulatory institutions, so equating tax with theft is unwelcome; inferred.

harm-principle.rationale: Bioconservatives hold that some uses of biotechnology, such as enhancement or cloning, should be limited even where no clear harm to others is shown, because of dignity and human nature, so a pure harm principle is rejected.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Fukuyama grounds rights in a shared species endowment and Habermas stresses the species' ethical self-understanding, which suggests adherents do not reduce morality to individual rights alone.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Fukuyama and Habermas ground legitimacy in democratic voice, so adherents lean against exit as the main check; inferred.

state-as-business.rationale: Fukuyama insists science and markets must serve ends set by political community, which runs against treating citizens as customers; inferred.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Fukuyama's Factor X holds that dignity rests on a shared human endowment rather than group differences, and bioconservative sources do not endorse racial hereditarianism; inferred.

total-state.rationale: Bioconservatives want democratic regulation of a specific domain, not state direction of all life; Habermas and Fukuyama defend liberal democracy.

national-rebirth.rationale: Not addressed; their caution about radical change implies disagreement.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Not addressed; inferred disagreement from their focus on restraint and humility.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Modern bioconservatives defend democratic law, so lord-and-vassal authority is not their model; inferred.

bound-labor.rationale: Kass's emphasis on dignity and humans not being treated as mere instruments rules out legally bound labour; inferred.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Fukuyama argues human nature and dignity rest on objective facts about the species and that regulators can tell pathology from normality, which counts against the claim; inferred.

universal-morality.rationale: Fukuyama and Kass seek a positive account of human nature and dignity that holds for all humans, and Habermas defends universal moral equality, so adherents lean to agree.

single-common-good.rationale: Adherents want shared deliberation on the human good, but they accept pluralism in democracy, so they are split on one rational common good.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Habermas and Fukuyama argue secularly while Kass's humane reasoning cites reverence and gratitude, so adherents do not share a single stance.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Bioconservatives value inherited human nature and the natural continuity of generations, so sacrificing inherited institutions is rejected by inference.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Kass emphasises natural sexual difference in procreation but the camp does not take positions on legal sex roles; Habermas and Sandel would oppose.

ban-interest.rationale: Not addressed; inferred disagreement because bioconservatives are not monetary radicals.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Fukuyama's Factor X and Habermas's moral equality hold that all humans share dignity, so racial segregation is incompatible with the view. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

elite-replacement.rationale: The sources contain no such claim and the main figures are mainstream scholars; inferred disagreement.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Not addressed by the sources; adherents are split.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Bioconservatives oppose genetic engineering of people and cite the eugenic past; Fukuyama and Habermas oppose state selection of human traits, so state discouragement of births by genetic status is rejected.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Bioconservatives require state regulation of biotechnology, which exceeds the night-watchman remit.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Fukuyama's shared-endowment account of human dignity and Habermas's moral equality contradict racial hierarchies. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Fukuyama's Factor X holds that all humans share an equal dignity rooted in a common endowment and Habermas treats genetic enhancement as a threat to moral equality, so equal worth is central.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Adherents argue on secular and liberal-democratic grounds, so legal restrictions on religious conversion are unlikely; inferred.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Not addressed; their acceptance of medical animal use and food suggests disagreement, inferred.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: Not addressed; liberal-democratic orientation implies disagreement.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Fukuyama holds that legitimate science policy must be decided by the democratic community acting through elected representatives, which supports the principle of consent.

population-transfer.rationale: Dignity of every human person is central, so forcing a minority to leave is incompatible with the view. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Not addressed; adherents accept state enforcement of biotech rules, so an absolute is not obviously theirs.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Kass warns that competitive pressure pushes people toward enhancement they would not otherwise choose, so adherents resist treating struggle as the main engine of progress.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Habermas's worry about asymmetrical parent-child domination is related, but adherents have no shared view on republican freedom; no direct statement.

separated-powers.rationale: Fukuyama favours institutional checks on biotech and democratic oversight; endorsement of separated powers is inferred from their liberal-democratic commitments.

vanguard-party.rationale: Not addressed; their democratic orientation suggests disagreement.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Fukuyama's emphasis on common human dignity is universalist, and the sources make no claim that diversity weakens cohesion; inferred.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Fukuyama stresses scientifically informed elected representatives, which runs against lottery; inferred.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Habermas and Fukuyama defend rights and the rule of law, so suspending protections is inferred as unwelcome.

party-controls-media.rationale: Democratic deliberation is the route Fukuyama and Habermas name for deciding technology policy, which requires free information; inferred.

party-commands-army.rationale: Not addressed; liberal-democratic orientation implies disagreement.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Fukuyama and Annas want international biotech rules, but broader supranational integration is not addressed.

clerical-rule.rationale: Bioconservatism argues from democratic and humanistic grounds, not clerical authority; inferred.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Not addressed; liberal-democratic figures like Habermas would reject, though Kass is more conservative.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: National reunification is never discussed in the bioconservative sources.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Not addressed; Fukuyama argues for universal human nature, but cultural ranking is not discussed.

death-penalty.rationale: Not addressed; adherents range from liberal to conservative.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Fukuyama and Kass ground their account of human nature in evolutionary biology, so adherents do not favour teaching creationism in public schools.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Kass is conservative on the degradation of sexuality but Habermas and Sandel are liberal; no common position.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Adherents defend dignity and democratic process, which suggests disagreement; inferred.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Not addressed directly; communitarian Sandel might agree, Kass and Fukuyama differ.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Bioconservatism urges caution and restraint toward novel biotechnologies even before outcomes are known, which is a precautionary stance, though the statement concerns environmental risks specifically. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Their case rests on the equal dignity of all humans and democratic legitimacy, which excludes a sacred ruler. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

character-from-environment.rationale: Fukuyama defines human nature as species-typical traits that come from genetics, not just environment, and Kass defends innate nature, so adherents lean against character being formed mainly by circumstance.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Fukuyama and Habermas place political authority within law and democratic accountability.

space-expansion.rationale: Not addressed, but transhumanist space visions are contrary to the bioconservative outlook; inferred.

leader-cult.rationale: Not addressed; inconsistent with their democratic-dignitarian commitments, inferred.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Not addressed; universalist dignity commitments imply disagreement.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Not addressed; the camp argues on liberal-democratic and humanistic grounds, so punishing apostasy is inferred as rejected.

women-must-cover.rationale: Not addressed; inferred disagreement from liberal-democratic commitments of leading figures.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Kass and Fukuyama treat technology and human nature as shaping ethics, but they do not reduce change to economic base; inferred mild disagreement.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Habermas defends constitutional democracy with rights that constrain majorities; inferred for the camp.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Trade treaty terms never come up in the bioconservative literature, so no stance is documented.

moral-incentives.rationale: The sources say nothing on incentives at work, and adherents do not share an economic doctrine.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Bioconservatives seek democratic and legal control of technology; guerrilla revolution is far from their method, inferred.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Habermas's equality argument leans toward abolition but Kass and Fukuyama are silent on titles, so adherents are unsettled.

history-own-civilization.rationale: School history teaching is outside the sources.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Fukuyama's shared-dignity universalism does not support ranking societies by advancement, though empire is never discussed.

patriotic-education.rationale: Civic education is never discussed by the sources.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Admissions policy is outside the literature; adherents split along their wider politics.

public-money-creation.rationale: Monetary policy never appears in the bioconservative sources.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: The sources do not address capitalism's crises.

delink-world-market.rationale: Development strategy never appears in these sources.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: Marxist theory of imperialism is not discussed.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Habermas's moral equality and Fukuyama's shared dignity imply opposition to licensed discrimination, though anti-discrimination law is never addressed.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Habermas and Fukuyama rest the case against enhancement on rights and dignity protected by constitutional order, so entrenched rights are inferred to be welcome.

elective-rulers.rationale: Fukuyama requires elected, informed representatives to decide biotech policy, so electing rulers fits, though hereditary monarchy is not discussed.

minority-veto.rationale: Fukuyama's call for democratic decisions binding on all, including international rules, contradicts a veto for each dissenter; inferred.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Bioconservatives defend nature and the moral weight of living beings, and nothing in them denies animal sentience, but the sources focus on humans so this is inferred.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Not addressed by the sources; the camp accepts medical use in principle but takes no stance on food or research limits.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Bioconservatives call for public democratic deliberation on biotechnology, so withdrawal from public affairs is not their ideal; inferred.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Kass worries about drugs and media making people content without effort, but the claim about social reproduction is Marxist and not shared.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Gramscian theory is not part of the sources.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Habermas leans to yes and Fukuyama is mixed; the literature does not discuss constitutional founding values.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Fukuyama is Cold War liberal but the sources do not address this comparison, so no stance is stated.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: The sources never address it, but the figures are mainstream scholars who would not deny slavery's role; inferred.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Fukuyama accepts cross-country variation in ethical views and political systems but still wants harmonised biotech rules; no clear stance on this claim.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Democratic control of institutions is stressed; inferred disagreement.

filial-duty.rationale: Kass writes about generational succession and obligations across the life cycle, which is consistent with filial duty, though he does not state it as a duty.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Fukuyama favours informed representatives deliberating, not mandated delegates; inferred.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Kass criticises the pursuit of satisfaction through products that bypass effort and meaning, so adherents lean toward seeing consumerist desire as harmful, though the sources do not discuss consumer goods in general.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Not addressed, but the camp's democratic and rights-based orientation suggests no support for intervention against an ally's sovereignty.

corporate-influence.rationale: Fukuyama says science and commerce must not set their own ends, which supports concern about corporate sway in biotech policy, though lobbying itself is not discussed.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Kass defends natural procreation and generational renewal but sets out no incentive policy.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Bioconservatives expect enforceable democratic regulation, so denying any duty to obey law runs against them; inferred.

non-intervention.rationale: Fukuyama and Annas argue for international rules binding states on biotech, which cuts against absolute non-intervention; inferred.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Equal dignity of all humans is central to the camp and no source supports conspiracy claims against a minority. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Kass defends natural family and generational continuity, so stripping marriage of legal standing is inferred as unwelcome.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Fukuyama wants informed democratic deliberation, which favours openness, but the legal right is not discussed.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Fukuyama and Annas call for international treaties on biotech that bind states, so primacy of national law over them is inferred as disfavoured.

defeat-communism.rationale: Fukuyama is associated with the Cold War liberal outlook but the sources here do not take this up.

religion-illusion.rationale: Kass, whose reasoning draws on reverence and gratitude toward life, would not call religion an illusion; Habermas is a secular but respectful, so mild disagreement.

socialized-care.rationale: Kass defends the family as the setting for child-rearing, but no source addresses public care provision.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Language policy is not a bioconservative subject.

majority-settlement.rationale: Dignity universalism makes ethnic settlement policies unlikely to be endorsed; inferred.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Bioconservatives cite eugenics and the Nazi past as warnings, and nothing in their sources questions the Holocaust; Habermas and Fukuyama are mainstream historians-aware scholars. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Not addressed; liberal members like Habermas and Sandel strongly reject, and Kass focuses on biotech, so disagreement is inferred.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Democratic deliberation is their prescribed route to governing biotech, so suppressing opposition is rejected.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Their arguments are made in secular, democratic terms, so punishing blasphemy is not their program; inferred.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Universal dignity points against; colonial rule is never discussed, so inferred.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Not addressed; their democratic framing implies rejection.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Habermas and Sandel favour public deliberation, but Fukuyama prefers informed representatives; split.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: Kass is conservative on bodily nature while Habermas and Sandel are liberal; no shared position.

assisted-dying.rationale: Kass's account of mortality as part of a flourishing life and his worry about technology mastering death suggest bioconservatives lean against assisted dying, although the source does not address it directly. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Not addressed; adherents span the spectrum, which Wikipedia's account of the camp notes only implicitly.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Not addressed; mainstream scholars among the figures would not endorse it.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Habermas and Fukuyama argue secularly and Fukuyama locates legitimacy in the democratic community, so divine authority is not the shared position.

social-market-economy.rationale: Not addressed; Fukuyama and Habermas are broadly compatible but Kass is not committed.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Elected representatives are the model; inferred disagreement.

property-franchise.rationale: Equal moral standing is central to Habermas and Fukuyama, which excludes a wealth-based franchise. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

domination-women-nature.rationale: Not addressed by the sources; it is an ecofeminist claim and the camp is not feminist as such, though it values nature.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Fukuyama and Habermas favour law made through democratic processes, so rule through public laws fits, though the sources do not discuss decrees.

racial-franchise.rationale: Equal dignity of all humans is central, ruling out limiting the franchise by race. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Not addressed; secular argument style implies no endorsement.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Equal dignity of all humans means targeting a religious minority is rejected. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Sandel and Habermas favour public deliberation on bioethics and the US Council model is deliberative, but the sources do not address randomly selected assemblies.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Not addressed directly; enhancement-driven inequality worries exist but not about wealth in general.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Kass's account of gratitude toward the given and reverence for life and Habermas's respect for religious sources both oppose coercive atheism.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Bioconservatives rely on enforcement of biotech law, so abolishing police is inferred as disfavoured.

vote-delegation.rationale: Fukuyama favours elected, informed representatives, not liquid delegation; inferred.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Bioconservatives share a worry about catastrophic technological outcomes, such as Fukuyama's comparison with nuclear weapons, but existential-risk language is more associated with their transhumanist opponents.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Not addressed; liberal-democratic orientation implies disagreement.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Kass values earned achievement over unearned results, which hints at agreement for work, but he does not address property income.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Not addressed; the camp does not take a pacifist stance.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: Fukuyama defines human nature as species-typical, biologically grounded traits and Kass defends natural embodiment and sexual procreation, so adherents reject that sex is a social construction.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Fukuyama and Habermas argue in secular, procedural terms, so a spiritual struggle between good and evil is not the framing; inferred.

god-not-male.rationale: Theological language is not addressed; religious and secular adherents differ.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Feminist theology is not part of the literature, and adherents range from religious conservatives to secular liberals.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Not addressed; universalist dignity implies disagreement.

family-wage.rationale: Kass defends the family but the sources never address wage levels.

faster-drug-approval.rationale: Kass notes FDA oversight and liability as existing checks on enhancement uses, and bioconservatives distrust rapid medicalisation, so faster approval is inferred as unwelcome even though therapy is accepted.

ageing-research-funding.rationale: Kass argues against radical life extension, saying finitude and generational succession are essential to human goods, so dramatically expanded funding to defeat ageing is rejected; modest therapeutic research on age-related disease is another matter.

person-over-state.rationale: Habermas and Fukuyama root dignity in each person, which supports not treating a person merely as a means, though the sources do not address state versus person generally.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Kass appeals to a positive account of human nature and dignity that goes beyond the material and draws on reverence, and Fukuyama's Factor X includes moral choice and consciousness, so adherents lean to agree.

gm-crops.rationale: Fukuyama and others focus on human genetic modification and treat other applications separately; no stated stance on crops.

racial-group-interests.rationale: The camp's account of shared humanity does not support separate racial interests; inferred.

communal-electorates.rationale: Not addressed; liberal-democratic equality suggests disagreement.

future-generations.rationale: Kass worries that changing human nature through biotechnology affects future generations and Fukuyama's concern is the posthuman future, so adherents lean to agree that heritage should be handed on intact, even though the statement is about the Earth. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Bioconservatism relies on strong democratic state institutions to regulate biotechnology, so smashing the state is rejected.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Fukuyama's Factor X and Kass's positive account of human nature are central to the position.

nature-as-capital.rationale: Bioconservatives defend human nature and dignity but the sources do not address pricing ecosystems, so adherents split.

sacred-nation.rationale: The sources do not discuss nationhood, and the thinkers range from conservative to liberal.

student-debt-relief.rationale: Student debt is outside bioconservatism, and its thinkers range from conservative to social-democratic.

internal-colonialism.rationale: Regional inequality is not addressed by the doctrine or its main thinkers.

public-service-media.rationale: Not addressed; Habermas favoured independent public communication while Kass and Fukuyama did not address it.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Bioconservatism does not address the unity of religions; Kass appeals to religious tradition but the thinkers include secular figures like Habermas, so adherents split.

farm-price-support.rationale: Farm policy is outside the bioconservative literature, and the leading figures span centre-left to neoconservative.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: Nuclear arms are outside the bioethical literature and the sources give no position.

workers-own-party.rationale: Party politics of class is outside the bioconservative literature, whose thinkers range from conservative to social democrat.

ban-fgm.rationale: Not addressed directly; inferred from the emphasis on human dignity and bodily integrity as grounded in a shared human nature, as in Fukuyama's Factor X.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Not addressed directly; inferred from the stress on equal human dignity (Factor X), though the literature does not discuss inheritance.

one-language-many-names.rationale: Language naming is outside the bioconservative literature and the sources give no position.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: Pollution policy is outside the literature; Fukuyama favours democratic state control of technology but nothing is stated on tort liability.

customary-chiefs-lawmaking.rationale: Chiefs in lawmaking are outside the literature, and the thinkers include both traditionalists and liberals.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: Bioconservatives urge restraint on technology for human nature, but their stated concern is human nature and not ecology, and the sources give no common position.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Criminal sentencing is outside the bioconservative literature, and its figures differ along ordinary political lines.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: Immigration and language are outside the bioconservative literature, and its figures differ along ordinary political lines.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: Union membership rules are outside the bioconservative literature, and its figures span the left and right, so no common line.

voter-id.rationale: Voter identification is not addressed by bioconservative writers; this is inferred as a split issue.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Bioethical writers do not address state recognition of religious interpretations; Kass draws on religious tradition while Habermas and Sandel are secular.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Fukuyama and Habermas want democratic deliberation to steer technology, but none state a view on whether democracy is purely procedural; inferred as split.

premarital-sex.rationale: Sexual morality is not part of the core bioconservative case; Kass is traditional while Sandel and Habermas are liberal.

internet-shutdowns.rationale: Inferred from the emphasis on democratic institutions and civil liberties among its leading thinkers; internet shutdowns are never discussed.

negative-income-tax.rationale: Welfare design is outside the literature, and its leading figures range from neoconservative to social democratic.

women-suffrage.rationale: Its thinkers accept liberal-democratic equal rights as the basis of dignity (Fukuyama's Factor X); suffrage itself is not discussed, so this is inferred.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: Inferred: Kass and Fukuyama treat religious tradition as a resource for human dignity, though the question is never addressed directly.

race-social-construct.rationale: Fukuyama defends a universal human nature and equal dignity, but the literature does not address the scientific status of racial categories.

gender-equality-agencies.rationale: Gender-equality institutions are not discussed by bioconservative writers, and its figures are split on such state programmes.

homestead-ownership.rationale: Bioconservative writers do not address how property is first acquired.

international-criminal-courts.rationale: Inferred: Fukuyama and Habermas favour international regulation and law above the nation, though trials of leaders are not discussed.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Inferred: Kass reads scripture as moral philosophy and Sandel, Habermas and Fukuyama argue on secular grounds, not literal inerrancy.

gendered-self-government.rationale: Inferred from Habermas and Sandel's egalitarian leanings; the sources do not discuss group self-rule.

defend-planned-state.rationale: Inferred: the thinkers range from conservative to social-democratic and none defend such states; not discussed.

indirect-election.rationale: The current is split and the sources do not address indirect election.

national-church-status.rationale: Inferred: the thinkers argue for democratic oversight on secular grounds and do not seek privileged church status.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: Not addressed; thinkers range from conservative to social-democratic.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: Not addressed by the sources; the thinkers hold no common line.

keep-colonial-borders.rationale: Not addressed and anachronistic for this current.

simple-living.rationale: Inferred from Kass's argument that finitude and limits give life meaning, which favours restraint over abundance, though simple self-sufficiency is not stated.

equal-conscription.rationale: Not addressed; the thinkers hold no common line.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: The thinkers range from conservative to social-democratic and the sources do not address homeland attachment.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: The thinkers stress human dignity and legal limits on technology; none address drug policy, but extrajudicial killing contradicts the dignity they defend.

close-ties-china.rationale: Not addressed by bioconservative thinkers; positions on foreign policy are left neutral.

protect-kin-minorities.rationale: Not addressed; the thinkers range from conservative to social-democratic.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: Not addressed by the sources; the thinkers disagree on economics.

self-ownership.rationale: Bioconservatives reject a purely self-owning, market-driven view of the body in enhancement debates, but the sources do not discuss the principle directly; inferred.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: Not addressed; the thinkers hold different economic views.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Not addressed; thinkers differ on welfare design.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Bioconservatives want democratic institutions to steer technology, which implies keeping parties and intermediary bodies; inferred.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Not addressed; thinkers range from conservative to social-democratic.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Not addressed by the sources; adherents differ on religion and politics.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: Bioconservatives hold that technology should be constrained by human nature and dignity rather than combined freely with progress, though the ancestral-values wording is not theirs.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from Habermas's and Sandel's liberal-egalitarian views, while Kass is more traditional, so split.

national-resource-control.rationale: Not addressed; thinkers do not have a common line on resource control.

distribution-by-process.rationale: Distributive justice is outside the bioethical literature and its figures range from libertarian-leaning to social-democratic.

financial-transactions-tax.rationale: Outside the bioconservative literature; its figures span left to right.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: Not addressed; the thinkers named hold varied views, so no common line exists.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Not addressed; the profile covers biotechnology and human dignity, not the authority of law.

automate-paid-work.rationale: Inferred from the bioconservative call for democratic steering of technology toward human ends rather than maximal adoption.

multipolar-world.rationale: Fukuyama argues for international regulation of biotechnology, which suggests a preference for shared institutions over independent power centres; weakly inferred.

labour-theory-of-value.rationale: Not addressed; economic theory lies outside the profile.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: Not addressed; the thinkers range from conservative to social-democratic.

material-over-identity.rationale: Not addressed; the profile takes no stance on left strategy.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: Not addressed; outside the profile's scope.

missingStatements.text: Parents should not be allowed to select or modify the genetic traits of their children beyond preventing disease.
missingStatements.rationale: Habermas, Sandel and Kass each oppose prenatal trait design as undermining the child's freedom and the parent-child relation, and the SEP entry gives this as a core bioconservative claim.

missingStatements.text: Aging and death are part of a good human life and should not be abolished.
missingStatements.rationale: Kass argues that finitude is the source of aspiration, love and virtue and opposes radical life extension.

missingStatements.text: Human genetic modification that can be passed to later generations should be prohibited by law.
missingStatements.rationale: Fukuyama argues for state control of biotechnology and Annas proposes a species-protection treaty to stop germline change that threatens human nature.

missingStatements.text: There is a shared human nature that grounds human dignity and rights and should not be redesigned.
missingStatements.rationale: Fukuyama's Factor X and Kass's positive account of human nature are central to the position.

notes: Adherents are politically heterogeneous (Kass and Fukuyama conservative or neoconservative, Sandel communitarian, Habermas social-democratic), so most answers outside bioethics are neutral or inferred. Many 0 answers reflect that split, not indifference.
